metaDescription: Six Eightree smart plugs compared, from the basic Smart Life plug to 5GHz, energy monitoring, SmartThings and outdoor models, with picks by home setup.
introParagraphs: Eightree makes low-key smart plugs that lean on the Smart Life app, so every model starts with the same routine. You download the app, let the phone find the plug over Bluetooth, and then link Alexa or Google Home from inside the app. Once that is done, voice commands, schedules and remote control all work without a hub.

The six picks here separate on band support, power rating, outlet layout and extras. We include the basic four pack, the 15A mini, a 5GHz model, a SmartThings version, a 5GHz plug with energy monitoring, and an outdoor plug with two independent outlets. Listings that differ only by pack count, like the one, two and four packs, were counted as one product.

We evaluated everything from product specs and buyer feedback, with extra attention to the setup path since that is where most owners get stuck. The goal is to match each plug to a real household instead of ranking them in the abstract.

products.name: EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug with Energy Monitoring
products.description:
The EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug with energy monitoring is the most capable plug in the brand's indoor range. It supports both 5GHz and 2.4GHz Wi-Fi, so pairing does not depend on forcing a phone onto the slower band. The listing also calls out an energy monitor that shows usage patterns, which no other pick here advertises.

The design is compact enough that the listing says two plugs can share one outlet at the same time. It is ETL and FCC certified and works with Alexa and Google Home. The extra insight into consumption helps when deciding whether a space fan or a lamp is worth leaving on a timer. The tradeoff is that the listing does not state an amperage or wattage in the part we reviewed, so check the housing before pairing a demanding appliance.

Setup follows the usual Smart Life routine, with the phone finding the plug and then linking voice assistants. Compared with the EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug 15A, this one adds energy data but gives up the explicit 15A and 1800W line. Next to the basic Smart Life model, it solves the 5GHz pairing problem. If seeing usage matters, it is the clear leader of the six.

products.name: EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug 15A
products.description:
The EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug 15A is the pick for people who want a clear power rating and a faster connection. It lists 120V and 15A, which equals 1800W, and it describes everyday loads such as lamps and fans plus higher-draw appliances like coffee makers. Bluetooth makes setup easy, and dual-band Wi-Fi gives a choice of band.

The 5GHz option promises quicker response times when the plug is near the router. Hands-free control works through Alexa or Google Home, which the listing says integrate seamlessly. As with any plug, the rating is a ceiling and heat-producing appliances deserve a careful read of their own labels. The compact body keeps neighbouring sockets usable in most cases.

This plug sits between the energy monitoring model and the basic one in capability. Compared with the EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug, which sticks to 2.4GHz, it gives more network flexibility, while compared with the monitoring model it states its rating more clearly. It does not list an energy meter or Matter support. Pick it when the router is close and the load is on the heavier side.
products.bestFor: Heavier everyday loads on a router that favors 5GHz.

products.name: EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug, Round Mini
products.description:
The EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug has a compact round shape that is only 1.2 inches thick. That makes it a good fit behind furniture or in narrow spaces where a bulky adapter would not clear the wall. The listing rates it at 15A and 1800W and mentions coffee makers, air fryers and heaters as high-power examples.

No hub is needed, and setup means downloading the Smart Life app, turning on Bluetooth and connecting to 2.4GHz Wi-Fi. The slim profile is the main reason to choose it over a blockier plug. The caution is that the listing names heaters, yet heat-producing loads strain any plug, so read the label of the appliance and the plug before relying on that. It does not list 5GHz, an energy meter or Matter.

Compared with the EIGHTREE Smart Plug Basic Four Pack, it states its rating plainly, which gives more confidence for kitchen use. Compared with the 5GHz 15A model, it is more limited in network flexibility. Both of those differences are small for a lamp or a fan. For a tight spot behind a sofa or a bed, the round mini is the most practical body of the six.

products.name: EIGHTREE Smart Plug WiFi Outlet, 15A, 4 Pack
products.description:
The EIGHTREE Smart Plug WiFi Outlet is the basic model that most buyers will see first. The listing says the phone's Bluetooth automatically finds the plug after you open the Smart Life app. Voice control with Alexa and Google Home works, but it requires linking through the Smart Life app first.

That extra link is the one thing to understand before buying, because the voice assistant does not pair with the plug directly. The listing explains the route through the app's third-party settings. It is available in single, two and four pack versions, all of which we treated as one product. The trade is a no-frills plug with few extras to learn.

It does not list 5GHz, an energy meter or a SmartThings route. Compared with the EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug, it lacks the slim round shape and the explicit 1800W line in the text we reviewed. Compared with the energy monitoring model, it is plainer and easier to understand. For a first plug in a home that already uses Alexa or Google, it does the job.

products.name: EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug with SmartThings
products.description:
The EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug with SmartThings support is aimed at Samsung households. It lists compatibility with Alexa, Google Home and SmartThings, and the listing says to follow setup instructions for a straightforward connection. Alexa voice control still requires linking the plug to the Smart Life app first.

The SmartThings tie-in is the main reason to choose it, since the other EIGHTREE plugs do not mention it. The listing also contains a note that something is not supported, which is cut off in the text we saw, so read the full page before buying for a specific feature. It is sold as a four pack. The plug fills out the family for households that already run SmartThings.

Setup mirrors the rest of the line, with Smart Life as the starting point. Compared with the EIGHTREE Smart Plug WiFi Outlet, it adds a platform, and compared with the 5GHz 15A model it lacks dual-band support. It does not list energy monitoring. For anyone with SmartThings hubs or phones, it removes a workaround.

products.name: EIGHTREE Outdoor Smart Plug, 2 Independent Outlets
products.description:
The EIGHTREE Outdoor Smart Plug brings two independent outlets to patios, porches and garden areas. The listing says each outlet is controlled separately, so patio lights and a fountain can run on different schedules. It carries an IP44 rating, which the maker describes as protection from rain splashes.

The listing also highlights an extended Wi-Fi range for large outdoor areas, which addresses the biggest outdoor frustration. IP44 means splash-proof and not submersible, so it still belongs under cover or shelter from heavy weather. A 15A rating is listed. The tradeoff is a larger body that suits outdoor outlets more than indoor ones.

Compared with the EIGHTREE Smart Plug WiFi Outlet, it adds weather protection and a second outlet. A 5GHz outdoor variant also exists in the brand lineup, but we counted that as a sibling and picked this one for its wider range claim. Pair this plug with a timer routine for holiday lights. It is the only outdoor-built choice of the six.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Every EIGHTREE plug in this comparison uses the Smart Life app as the starting point, and voice assistants link from inside it. The EIGHTREE Smart Plug WiFi Outlet listing spells out the third-party route for Alexa and Google Home. Plugs from white-label brands often route through Smart Life or Tuya before linking to voice assistants, so expect a short extra step. If the maker shuts down its cloud service, remote control can stop working. For a relative who dislikes apps, set up the voice names and schedules once, then leave it alone.

Nearly all Wi-Fi plugs connect to 2.4GHz only, so a phone on 5GHz can fail during setup. The EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug 15A and the 5GHz energy monitoring model list both bands, which avoids that problem. The EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug and the basic four pack stay with 2.4GHz. Choose 5GHz when the plug sits close to the router, and choose 2.4GHz when it must reach through several walls. A plug in the far end of a house is the situation where 2.4GHz still wins.

A clear rating tells you what the plug can safely carry. The EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug 15A and the EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug both state 15A and 1800W, while some listings only imply a rating. Look for ETL or UL on the housing, which the monitoring model lists as ETL and FCC. Heat-producing loads such as space heaters strain any plug, even when the listing names them. Check the appliance label in watts before you commit.

An energy monitor turns a plug into a small diagnostic tool, showing how much power a device draws over time. Among the six, only the EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug with energy monitoring lists it. That helps with space fans, window units on a timer or old appliances you suspect are wasteful. Energy data often stays in the brand app and may not pass through other platforms. If you will never check it, skip the premium and pick a simpler plug.

A compact body that leaves the second outlet free matters on a wall duplex, because bulky plugs block it. The EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug is only 1.2 inches thick and round, and the monitoring model is described as letting two plugs share one outlet. Measure the clearance behind a bed or sofa before you buy. A slim plug also pulls less on the outlet in an older wall. Outdoor models are naturally larger.

Outdoor use needs a weather rating, and the EIGHTREE Outdoor Smart Plug is the only one here with IP44. IP44 handles splashes, so it still wants a covered spot away from standing water. The two independent outlets let patio lights and a fountain follow different schedules. Indoor plugs should stay indoors, even under a porch roof. When in doubt, pick the outdoor model for any space where moisture can reach.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup and app path
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at how each plug reaches a working state. All six rely on the Smart Life app and Bluetooth discovery, so the difference lies in the band options. The two 5GHz plugs avoid the common 2.4GHz-only pairing snag. The basic four pack and the 15A mini follow the standard path.

howWeEvaluated.title: Rating clarity
howWeEvaluated.description: This category rewards a listing that states amperage and certifications. The EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug 15A and the EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug both state 15A and 1800W. The monitoring plug lists ETL and FCC. The basic four pack and SmartThings model are less specific about wattage.

howWeEvaluated.title: Features beyond on and off
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared extras such as energy monitoring, SmartThings support and independent outlets. The monitoring model leads on data, the SmartThings model leads on platform reach, and the outdoor plug leads on outlet count. None of the six lists Matter. The mix gives each household a clear reason to pick.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit in tight or outdoor spaces
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked body size and weather ratings. The round 15A mini is 1.2 inches thick, and the outdoor model carries IP44. The monitoring plug claims two plugs per outlet. Indoor standard bodies score in the middle.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value across pack sizes
howWeEvaluated.description: Multi-packs lower the cost per plug but only help if you use several. Most of the indoor listings come in packs of one, two or four. The outdoor plug is a single purchase, and that suits its narrow use. We rewarded plugs whose extras match a real need.

faq.q: Why do I have to use the Smart Life app?
faq.a: EIGHTREE plugs run on the Smart Life platform, so the app is where the plug is added, named and scheduled. Alexa and Google Home link from inside it through the third-party settings. That is a normal pattern for white-label plugs. After setup, daily use often happens by voice only.

faq.q: Which EIGHTREE plug works on 5GHz Wi-Fi?
faq.a: The EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug 15A and the EIGHTREE 5GHz Smart Plug with energy monitoring list both bands. The EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug and the basic four pack describe 2.4GHz. If your phone is on 5GHz, the dual-band picks avoid the switching step. Once paired, any of them runs from the app.

faq.q: Can I run a coffee maker or air fryer on it?
faq.a: The EIGHTREE 15A Smart Plug lists coffee makers and air fryers as examples of high-power devices at 15A and 1800W. Read the appliance label and keep the load under the rating. The device must also have a physical switch left on. Heaters need extra caution because continuous heat strains any plug.

faq.q: Does the outdoor plug survive rain?
faq.a: It carries an IP44 rating, which the maker describes as protection against splashes and light moisture. That is not the same as fully waterproof, so keep it under cover and out of standing water. The two outlets work independently. Bring it indoors if a storm brings flooding or heavy driving rain.

faq.q: Is a four pack worth it?
faq.a: A four pack lowers the cost per plug, but only if you have four real jobs for them. Lamps, a fan, a coffee maker and holiday lights are typical first uses. Buying one first lets you learn the app. Extras can be added later.

faq.q: Do these plugs work with Apple Home?
faq.a: None of the listings we reviewed mentions Apple Home or Matter. They list Alexa and Google Home, and one lists SmartThings. Apple households should pick a Matter plug from another range. The EIGHTREE plugs fit best in Alexa and Google homes.

faq.q: What happens if the internet goes down?
faq.a: These plugs depend on a cloud service for remote control and voice commands, so they may stop responding without internet. Schedules saved on the plug can sometimes keep running, but check how yours behaves. A Matter plug is better if local control matters. Keep a manual option for anything that matters, such as a heating device.
